articles.title: BoC’s Gravelle says policy scenarios help build credibility
articles.expand: Bank of Canada Deputy Governor Toni Gravelle discussed how the central bank uses scenarios to explain how it might respond as economic conditions change. Bank of Canada scenarios are designed to help keep the BoC accountable and build credibility. When the public trusts the BoC to keep inflation around 2%, their inflation expectations stay anchored. If inflation expectations are anchored, that makes monetary policy more effective. By helping market participants understand how we tend to react when conditions change, we can shape their expectations. Bank of Canada says scenarios help make monet...

articles.expand: Fed Governor Chris Waller came out hawkish on CNBC this morning. He wants to break the psychology that 3% inflation is normal. He has pointed out that more than 70% of core PCE services components were running above 3% year over year in September, and he worries that demand is still firm enough for businesses to pass along price increases. His message for December was direct. If the Fed is unwilling to signal a faster pace of hikes in its statement or press conference, he favors a 50-basis-point move at the meeting. A firm jobs number would challenge that, lifting front-end yields and supporting the currency, while a rise in unemployment would reinforce bets on easing by 2027. The contrast between strong wage growth and rising layoffs creates two-way risk for Australian bank stocks and rate-sensitive retailers, especially given the job cuts at David Jones and Bunnings. articles.expand: Record exports support the view that Japan’s economy can absorb a December rate hike despite the third-quarter contraction, which should keep upward pressure on short-end JGB yields. Chipmakers and chip equipment suppliers in Tokyo are the clearest beneficiaries, though the reliance on AI demand leaves them exposed to any pullback in global tech spending. Oil is the swing factor for the trade balance: crude prices tied to the Iran war set the size of Japan’s import bill, and a renewed spike would quickly widen the deficit. articles.title: Australian wages jump 1.1%, strongest since 2023, but real pay falls for a fourth quarter
articles.expand: The headline beat should support the Australian dollar and short-dated yields at the margin, as traders reassess how firmly they had ruled out another RBA hike. The detail limits the hawkish case, though. Private sector strength came from a one-off award decision, public sector pay is doing much of the work, and real wages are still falling, so it’s hard to argue wages are driving inflation. That mix makes a large repricing of December less likely. For AUD/USD, rate expectations at home are still competing with a Fed on a hiking path. --- Preview here: Economic and event calendar in Asia 18 No...

articles.title: Japan’s trade deficit comes in at half the expected size as exports jump 20.5%
articles.expand: The narrower deficit is mildly supportive for the yen because it reduces the yen sold to pay for imports. Rate differentials still dominate, though, and USD/JPY remains pinned near 160 while the Fed is on a hiking path. Oil is the key swing factor: Japan’s import bill is highly sensitive to crude prices during the Iran war, so any renewed rise in oil would quickly reverse today’s improvement. For the BOJ, the data adds to evidence that the economy can absorb a December hike, which could nudge short-end JGB yields higher. Exporters with heavy chip exposure should find support in Tokyo trade. --...

articles.title: Kuroda, once Japan’s great easer, says BOJ rates may need to rise above neutral
articles.expand: For Japanese rates and the yen, a call for above-neutral rates from the architect of Japan’s easing era adds weight to the hawkish tail of BOJ pricing. Most economists see a terminal rate near 1.75%, and talk of 2.5% now has a high-profile backer. Kuroda no longer sets policy, so the direct effect is limited. Still, his critique of the food tax cut puts the fiscal-monetary tension in sharp relief ahead of an expected December hike. Front-end JGB yields, with the two-year near 1.88%, are most exposed to any shift toward a higher peak. Oil matters here too. Kuroda explicitly links Japan’s inflat...

articles.title: NZ 1-year inflation expectations jump to 2.9%, but the 2-year anchor barely moves
articles.expand: For the RBNZ, the survey is mixed rather than alarming. The stable two-year reading lets policymakers argue that expectations remain anchored. The one-year jump and the higher OCR expectations show forecasters now firmly expect tightening. That supports pricing for a hike at the 9 December Monetary Policy Statement, and any pushback from the RBNZ would surprise. For the New Zealand dollar, near 0.55, higher rate expectations give some support, though the move in the two-year gauge is too small to be a strong driver on its own. articles.title: RBA minutes: 6 members saw rates “not clearly sufficient”, 3 warned of sharper downturn
articles.expand: On balance the minutes lean hawkish, unsurpisngly. The majority’s view that 4.85% is “not clearly sufficient” sits awkwardly with market pricing that had all but ruled out further hikes, and it backs up Bullock’s comment this morning about upside risks. The minority’s warning of a sharper downturn sets a high bar for a December move, though. This week’s wage and jobs data, and the October CPI jump the staff flagged in advance, matter more than usual. For the Australian dollar, near 0.6730, the minutes are mildly supportive but unlikely to change the trend while policy diverges from the Fed. Th...

articles.title: RBA’s Bullock says inflation risks still skewed to upside ahead of 6-3 vote minutes
articles.expand: Bullock’s comment pushes back modestly against market pricing that has all but ruled out a December hike. It could offer the Australian dollar some support after it fell this week to its lowest level since late January. One line on a panel is unlikely to shift pricing on its own, so the minutes are the bigger test. Any sign that the majority on the board saw a real chance of further tightening would firm up the hawkish reading of Bullock’s remarks. If the minutes play up how close the vote was, front-end rates may decide the governor’s comment is a hedge, not a signal. - Minutes preview here: ...

articles.title: New Zealand food prices fall 0.4% in October as RBNZ flags 3 rising global risks
articles.expand: Neither release is likely to move the New Zealand dollar much on its own. The Financial Stability Report assesses risk rather than signalling policy, and the food price data is only a small input into quarterly inflation. The RBNZ’s warning that recent cost pressures and higher interest rates could reverse the easing in domestic stress points in a cautious direction. Its list of global risks, from Middle East energy disruption to an AI valuation correction, reads like a list of the shocks that tend to hurt risk-sensitive currencies like the kiwi. --- Coming up later from neighbouring Australia...
